newsitem.title: INDIA: India communists strongly oppose oil price hikes.
newsitem.headline: India communists strongly oppose oil price hikes.

text.p: India's main communist parties, partners in the ruling United Front coalition, said they would reiterate their opposition to any proposal to raise petroleum product prices at a meeting later on Monday.
The United Front's policy-making Steering Committee is scheduled to meet at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) to discuss the sensitive issue.
"We are still opposing the increases. We have not changed our stance," Sitaram Yechury, a leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI) and a member of the Steering Committee, told Reuters.
Yechury denied a news agency report that the CPI was not opposed to a proposal for raising petroleum product prices.
"We want the government to see other options," said D. Raja, a leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI) and another member of the Steering Committee.
"We oppose the oil price hike. It is an easy way out, yielding to the pressures of the market forces."

The CPI has submitted an alternative plan to the Steering Committee that seeks to avoid what it views as a crippling rise in oil prices and calls for the government to return to the state-run oil sector surplus funds taken from it by earlier governments.
It also wants key customs and excise duties eliminated. Any increase in prices this week would be the second by the United Front coalition in its one year in power.

Last July the government raised the price of gasoline by 25 percent, and prices of high-speed diesel, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for cooking, paraffin wax and fuel oil by 30 percent. It was forced to scale back the rise in diesel prices to 15 percent after nationwide protests.
United Front leaders have consistently blamed the previous Congress government for not raising the prices of petroleun products in the last two-and-half years of the Congress rule.
The previous Congress government's only increase in the prices of gasoline and diesel was in February 1994.

As of the end of March domestic oil firms were owed 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) from the oil pool account deficit, which represents the amount owed by the government to the companies for selling below market prices. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
